actSpeakBrief: Describing a line you cannot see is the fastest way to find out whether your trend language is doing any work.
actSpeak1: Describe one of the two lines aloud, without figures and without naming the device. Your partner draws it. Compare, then swap.
actSpeak2: Argue for two minutes that the printer line is the more interesting one, then swap and argue for the speaker line.
actSpeak3: One of you says a trend sentence with a verb. The other says it again as a noun phrase. Keep going until one of you stalls.
actWriteBrief: Write the full report for this graph: introduction, overview, and one body paragraph per line. Quote no more than six figures in total, and use both trend grammars at least once each.
coverSub: Task 1’s commonest chart after the bar. Direction, degree and tense — and how to describe a decade without describing every point on it.
s1Title: A line graph is about change over time
s1ColA: A bar chart compares things. A line graph shows what happened to them. So the overview names the direction each line took, and the body describes the stages of that movement.
s1ColB: Everything follows from that. The verbs are movement verbs, the adverbs are speed, and the tense is decided by the dates printed on the axis — not by anything you choose.
s1Note: The commonest failure is not vocabulary. It is describing every point — a report that walks through twelve readings in order has no overview and no grouping, and it will not reach band 6.
s3Title: Two ways to say the same movement
s3ColA:
Verb + adverb.
Printer ownership fell steadily.
Smart speakers rose sharply.
s3ColB:
There was a + adjective + noun.
There was a steady fall in printer ownership.
There was a sharp rise in smart speakers.
s3Note: Same fact, two grammars. Using both across a report is what Lexical Resource rewards — using one of them six times is what caps it.
s6ColA: Sharply / steeply. A lot, quickly. Speakers after 2016.
s6ColB: Steadily. At about the same rate throughout. Printers.
s6ColD: Slightly / marginally. Only a little. Speakers before 2014.
s6Note: Steadily does not mean slowly. It means at a constant rate, and it is the word most often misused — a steep, even fall is a steady one.
s9Ctx: Same two facts, the other grammar. This is the swap that widens Lexical Resource.
s10Ctx: Click a shape on the left, then the verb that describes it.
s12Ctx: One stage, one figure, one comparison. Click the parts in order.
x06a: Accurate, and it is a body sentence. An overview says what happened overall; this reports two readings from one year.
x06b: Both directions, plus the one event that matters — the overtake. No figures, which is right: the numbers are the body's work.
x06c: One line only. An overview has to cover the whole chart, and half of this chart is the line that is rising.
x06d: Announcing the topic is not summarising it. This sentence would sit above any chart at all and tells a reader nothing.
x07a: The graph shows is present, and that is right in the introduction. But the data happened between 2010 and 2020, so the trends themselves go in the past: fell, rose.
x07b: Mixing them is exactly the error this question exists to prevent. One time frame on the axis means one tense in the report.
x07c: Nothing on this chart is projected. Future forms belong only where the axis itself carries future dates or the label says estimated.
x07d: The dates decide it, and here they are all finished, so every trend in the report is past simple. Nothing about your own opinion or the writing date comes into it.
x09a: You can see that it happened and you cannot see when. Saying so exactly is accuracy, and accuracy is marked. Inventing 2019 is not.
x09b: 2019 is not on the chart. It is a reasonable guess and it is still a figure you did not read, which is the definition of inaccurate reporting.
x09c: The crossing is the single most notable event on the graph. Leaving it out is the opposite problem — a report that describes lines and misses what they did to each other.
x09d: They did cross, and a reader can see it. What is unknown is the date, not the fact — those are two different kinds of uncertainty.
x10a: Steadily — the fall is almost the same size every two years, which is what steady means. Not sharply: 32 points over ten years is not sudden.
x10b: Sharply or steeply — from 11% to 46% in four years. Before 2014 the same line was barely moving, and describing both is what earns the mark.
x11a: Decline, fall, decrease or drop. Note the adverb became an adjective: fell steadily → a steady fall.
x11b: Rise, increase, jump or surge — not growth, which does not take a. Saw is worth stealing too — it lets a date be the subject of the sentence and varies your openings.
x12a: Plateaued and fluctuated are the two worth learning properly: one means it stopped moving, the other means it never stopped. Candidates reach for fluctuated for any line that is not straight, and it is wrong unless the line changes direction more than once.
x13a: Twelve readings in order is the commonest Task 1 failure. It has no grouping, so Coherence suffers, and it runs out of words before the second line.
x13b: Half the chart missing is half the task missing. Task Achievement asks you to cover what is there, not what is interesting.
x13c: Group by what the line does, not by date. One paragraph per line, each built around its turning point, uses every number that matters and none that does not.
x13d: Figures are required in the body — that is where they belong. A body with no data at all is an overview written twice.
x14a: Two stages in one sentence, joined at the turning point by before. Two figures, and both matter — the one that shows how little had happened, and the one that shows how much did.
x15a: Over the period is standard and correct here, and it is a useful phrase precisely because it avoids repeating the dates.
x15b: Both figures are read correctly off the chart. The numbers are not the problem in this sentence.
x15c: Ownership is a good paraphrase of what the axis measures and does exactly the job an introduction wants.
x15d: Fluctuated means it changed direction repeatedly. This line only ever goes down, so the word contradicts the chart — an accuracy error, not a style one.
x16a: Past for what happened, future forms for what is projected, and the change of tense is itself the signal that you understood the label. This is a cheap grammar mark.
x16b: A projection is not a fact. Reporting it in the past states that something happened which has not happened yet.
x16c: The years to 2020 are recorded, not predicted. Putting them in the future misreports the half of the chart that is certain.
x16d: Present continuous describes something in progress now. A decade of readings is neither in progress nor now.
